name: Antihemorrhagic styptic

lead: A styptic is an astringent applied to small cuts to stop bleeding. In grooming, the styptic pencil or alum block is a shaving-kit staple for nicks.
The appearance payoff is cleaner post-shave skin: bleeding stops quickly, so there are fewer spots and tissue-paper patches.

paras: The stick or block is touched to the bleeding nick. Styptic pencils usually contain anhydrous aluminium sulfate, which contracts tissue and narrows blood vessels.
It can sting. Users with sensitive skin may react, and it is intended for minor wounds only.

angle.text: A styptic stops shaving nicks fast, leaving a smoother, less blemished look right after shaving.

lead: Styptics are astringent agents that stop bleeding. A styptic pencil is a short stick whose main ingredient is anhydrous aluminium sulfate; it works by contracting tissue to seal injured vessels.[1] Before safety razors, it was a standard shaving-kit item, and some people still use it on razor nicks.[1]

In looksmaxxing and grooming, it is used so shaving cuts stop bleeding quickly and heal without prominent marks. Styptic use stretches back centuries: reviews trace astringent plant drugs for bleeding through ancient and medieval medicine.[2]

paras: The astringent causes local vasoconstriction, and its high ionic strength promotes clumping of blood.[1] Other topical haemostatic agents include kaolin, chitosan and collagen products used in dressings.[1][3]

Reviews describe astringent drugs for bleeding in historical medicine, including the Maltese mushroom, which became a commodity after the Siege of Malta and later declined.[2] Nineteenth-century medical journals carried notices of new styptics, cotton and collodion preparations.[4]

No studies found on styptic pencils for shaving nicks. Related research includes a pilot randomised trial of an aluminium triformate mouthrinse, described as styptic and astringent, in periodontal patients.[5]
